query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A laser-cladded refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) coating with an optimized composition (elevated Cr and Al contents) will form a self-healing passivating oxide (e.g., alumina and/or chromia) during exposure to molten aluminum, thereby protecting the underlying substrate from erosion during hot dip aluminum plating.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional metallic parts (e.g., steel components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates) that are prone to rapid degradation when in direct contact with high‐temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.intervention: Apply a laser cladding deposition of a RHEA coating, specifically tailored with increased Cr/Al content to promote formation of a passivating oxide layer.
generation.conditions: Long-term, high-temperature exposure to liquid aluminum in the hot dip plating process.
generation.structural_mediator: The RHEA coating develops a dense, adherent, and self-healing oxide scale at its surface, ensuring good metallurgical bonding with the substrate and creating an effective barrier against molten aluminum.
generation.mechanism: Elevated Cr and Al in the coating oxidize in situ to form protective chromia and alumina layers that hinder further chemical attack and erosion by the molten aluminum. The inherent refractory nature and high-entropy effects provide thermal stability and structural integrity under extreme conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated parts will exhibit significantly improved corrosion and erosion resistance compared to uncoated parts, thereby extending the service life of the dipping and plating equipment.
generation.baseline: Uncoated conventional metallic components that corrode rapidly when exposed to high-temperature liquid aluminum in the plating process.
generation.boundary: The coating’s effectiveness is anticipated under typical hot dip plating conditions; however, performance under extreme cyclic thermal stresses or unforeseen chemical interactions still requires further validation.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvement figures (e.g., exact percentage reduction in erosion or extension of service life) and long-term cyclic performance need to be experimentally confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of plating equipment parts made from a conventional substrate: one group will receive the laser-cladded RHEA coating and the other will be left uncoated. Subject both groups to prolonged exposure in a hot dip aluminum plating process under identical conditions.
measurements: Rate of mass loss or weight change after defined exposure intervals
Surface morphology and oxide scale characterization via SEM/EDS
Thickness and integrity of the oxide layer using cross-sectional microscopy
Adhesion strength testing between the coating and substrate
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated parts do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion/erosion (i.e., similar mass loss, oxide layer deterioration, or failure of adhesion) compared to the uncoated parts, then the hypothesis is considered disproven.

frame.goal: To identify or design a protective material for preparatory parts that can resist erosion/corrosion by molten aluminum during the plating process.

decision.trend: Early work in high‐temperature environments relied on conventional metallic parts, which proved vulnerable to rapid degradation in the presence of corrosive molten aluminum. Over the past few years researchers have shifted toward advanced alloys—particularly refractory or high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coatings produced by methods such as laser cladding and sputtering—that not only offer high melting points but also have the ability to form dense, passivating oxides or protective phases under aggressive conditions. While such coatings have demonstrated excellent oxidation and wear resistance at elevated temperatures, they have been mainly validated in air or inert environments. The progress has been sequential: first attempts with standard metals were abandoned; next, composition‐tailored HEAs and composite coatings were developed to improve oxidation, wear, and corrosion resistance at high temperatures; however, none have yet fully addressed exposure to long‐term direct contact with molten aluminum.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved challenge is to develop a protective material (or coating) that not only withstands high-temperature exposure but also resists the chemical attack by long-term contact with molten aluminum—in other words, maintaining integrity and adhesion while preventing erosion in a very aggressive environment.
decision.lever: laser cladding deposition of a refractory high-entropy alloy coating with an optimized composition (e.g., elevated Cr/Al content) designed to form a self-healing/passivating oxide layer
decision.why: Because recent trends in HEA coatings have shown that surface-engineered layers can significantly enhance oxidation and wear performance at high temperatures. Tailoring the coating’s composition to promote the in-situ formation of a protective oxide scale is a logical next step to achieve durable, molten aluminum–resistant surfaces, thereby addressing the gap left by conventional metals.
